turn_text: And another issue making the rounds up here is, in terms of the Northern border, I know both the Senators, Tester, and Danes recently sent a letter to a Senate Appropriations Committee, they're asking for more funding for the Northern border. Here in Haver, the Wild Horse Port is not opening for the summer hours, it's just the normal eight to five. And definitely, and the Chief, excuse me, the Port of Chief Mountain over by Glacier is closed indefinitely. It sounds like it's probably not going to be opening for the season. What have you and what can you do as governor to try to find a solution here?

Well, I've brought Customs and Border Patrol folks together multiple times up there. This is an ongoing battle. We need to keep these ports open. They're critical to commerce for family relationships and while I was up and up along the Canadian border in Montana, you know, I spoke with families who, you know, have grandparents across the border, the families are actually split. This has dramatic impact when these hours are restricted. We need to keep these ports open and we'll continue to advocate for it.

And the Canadian government recently announced through at least the end of this month, they're still having the vaccination requirement to cross the border if people don't want to quarantine for 14 days. Have any thoughts on that? Are you going to continue to push to end that requirement?

Well, I joined with the premier of Alberta. Many other border states here. We wrote to both Joe Biden and Trudeau saying, guys, come on, open it up. You can do this. There's no reason why there are reasonable precautions that could be taken to continue to perpetuate this economic pandemic that they've created to try and deal with the health care issue. It just doesn't make any sense. So I just wish that there could be a little more common sense applied. We could get this border open back up and remove these restrictions.

turn_text: And in terms of fires season, you know, with summer just starting, I know you received the annual fire briefing pretty recently. What's the kind of outlook on on fires here in the state and what can people do to prevent a majority of fires are human started?

Yeah, that's right. About 80% of the wildland fires we see in Montana are human cause. So my first ask for everybody is when you're out in the woods, recreating along the river, just be careful. Please take precautions. Just be careful of open flames and everything else that can spark these fires. I did have the briefing. I had all our federal partners and state resources together in one room, and here's the bottom line. We look a little better than last year, but it's still really dry out there. So the two things the state's doing, one, we need to start managing our forests again, and I'm proud to Share with you, Josh, that we doubled the number of acres under active forest management last year to this year and a single year. We're going to continue to expand that using the good neighbor authority. We need to be better stewards of the forest. And then secondly, when fires start and they will, we're pursuing an aggressive attack approach to all fires under state control. Last year, 95% of the fires that started that were under state control we kept to less than 10 acres. I've encouraged our federal partners, both the Forest Service and BLM, to adopt the same policy. We're still working out the details on that, but we need to, when conditions are dry and our homes, our communities, our forests are at risk, we need to be aggressive in attacking these fires and put them out while they're still small.

Okay. And then lastly, while I've got you here, I know you were visiting the Highline last month as part of your 56 County tour. Can you tell everybody kind of what you learned from the tour and how you're going to use that knowledge as governor?

Well, I'll say first, I love getting out. I hired a good team at the agencies. I get them lined out on Mondays and I traveled the state the rest of the week. So I was up in Hill County, Blaine County, I was back up in Cascade County. In Hill, I met with teachers to discuss the Teach Act. I was encouraged. A number of them shared with me that they took the jobs as entry-level teachers because of the Teach Act. It bumped their pay about $3,500. We had 450 teachers statewide take advantage of the Teach Act. That was great. Over in Blaine County, I presented Haley Mitchell, a spirit of Montana award there at the Chinook High School. And boy, that was fun. Her whole family was there. She showed real entrepreneurial spirit. And it was great to be able to go and honor her. In terms of the round tables and discussions with county commissioners and farmers and ranchers and law enforcement, clearly it's dry. We need to continue to pray for rain. People are concerned about inflation. We continue to call on the Biden administration to shut off the spigot of spending that's making every one of our dollars. go less far, and to abandon this anti-American energy policy that's shut down, the Keystone XL, and is driving gasoline and diesel prices through the roof. So there's optimism. Montanans are resilient. We're excited about the moisture we've been getting in certain portions of the state. Certainly we need more up along the high line. But I think our best days are ahead of us.
